claim: Work domain analysis builds a means-ends model of the job (five abstraction levels: purpose, abstract function, general function, physical function, physical form), first of five cognitive work analysis phases. The method is well documented but descriptive; it gives no pass/fail rule.
agent_test: Compare an S0 gate that lists goals, constraints and decisions of the task against a plain gate, at equal tokens, on a mixed-class item set.

claim: No study found in 2020-2026 that uses Rasmussen-style work domain analysis or the abstraction hierarchy as a prompting or agent method and measures it against a baseline. Three independent search passes found zero hits (one review hit, Simkute 2024). Gap search added the nearest tested relatives (Step-Back, Self-Discover) but neither uses a multi-level means-ends hierarchy.
agent_test: Run the first test: abstraction-hierarchy prompt (purpose down to form, with why/how links) versus plain prompt, same tokens.

claim: Ecological displays built on work-domain constraints help human operators in several simulator studies, but evidence is mixed and often preliminary: workload gains in 3 of 5 AR-HUD scenarios, better helicopter landing control, subjective-only or null results elsewhere.
agent_test: Not directly testable on an agent; use only as a prior that constraint-visible representations help most on novel cases.

claim: Across 56 display evaluations, only iterative evaluation with end users separated successes (14/14 vs 13/22, p<0.01). Making functional relationships visible (EID) was not a significant predictor, and two or more design processes did not reach significance (17/20 vs 10/16, p=0.15).
agent_test: Treat the analysis as needing a check loop: compare an S0 analysis with and without a verify-against-examples pass.

claim: Positive results shrink in real settings: 53% (9/17) of novel displays were positive in clinical trials versus 75% (27/36) in simulated tasks.
agent_test: Expect S0 gains on a benchmark to be larger than on live tasks; hold out a deployment-style set.

claim: Expert decision models taken from task analysis, when given to an LLM, raise output quality: +76% preferred and +80% useful for GPT-4 in tutoring (700 conversations, p<0.05); an expert decision-ladder rule list raised coverage from 24.9% to 44.1% in quantum chemistry (not re-verified); recognition-primed prompts lifted care-seeking accuracy from 63.3% to 67.6%. Controls are weak and each is one domain.
agent_test: Equal-token test: expert-decision scaffold vs same-length generic advice vs none, on tasks where an expert decision list exists.

claim: Letting the model pick its own decision path helps strong models (GPT-4, llama-2) but not gpt-3.5; random decisions cut quality by 97% against expert decisions, so a wrong problem decomposition is worse than none.
agent_test: Test self-chosen vs given vs random problem-class labels at the S0 gate; measure harm from a wrong class.

claim: A recipe from a full cognitive work analysis changed LLM behaviour strongly (question-count incidence ratio 0.004 plain vs recipe) but moved similarity to a gold answer only a little (d=0.225, 95% CI 0.150 to 0.300), on 1,200 simulated exchanges with GPT-4o-mini and no test with children.
agent_test: Check whether behaviour change from a scaffold turns into accuracy change, not only style change.

claim: Prompts that reflect how experts decide under uncertainty improve accuracy mostly on the rare class (self-care 13.4% to 29.8% and 24.6%) while the 2 emergency and 30 non-emergency cases stayed high; only 45 vignettes, 13 of them self-care.
agent_test: Report per-class accuracy; test whether S0 class labels help rare classes at equal tokens.

claim: A typed, bounded, abstraction-layered agent memory beats flat memory; flat memory of concrete procedures can be worse than none (AppWorld Test-Normal 30.4 vs 62.8 memoryless). Gains are noisy where categories are small; the Test-Challenge comparison is confounded by scale and application mix (authors say so).
agent_test: Compare flat vs layered (purpose, workflow, unit) notes at equal injected lines.

claim: Task-level work taxonomies (O*NET) now define LLM benchmarks, and agents are far from doing complete work: best TheAgentCompany agent 30.3% (175 tasks); Claude Opus 4.1 47.6% win-or-tie against experts on GDPval gold (220 tasks, 44 occupations).
agent_test: Use a work-task benchmark as the held-out check for problem-class gating; report by task type.

claim: A check-your-deliverable prompt plus best-of-4 with a judge raised GPT-5's human win rate by 5 points on work tasks and cut egregious PowerPoint errors from 86% to 64%.
agent_test: Equal-token comparison of a verify prompt against best-of-N.

claim: Workers want more human agency than AI experts judge necessary: 47.5% of tasks sit where workers prefer more human involvement; 45.2% of occupations have H3 (equal partnership) as dominant level; 41.0% of startup task mappings fall in low-priority or red-light zones. Observed Claude use is below exposure forecasts (about 57% of occupations at 10% of tasks vs about 80% of workers forecast).
agent_test: Not an agent test. Use only to decide when the agent should ask the human (ask-or-act rule at S0).

claim: The abstraction hierarchy has no rules for which fact belongs on which level or for validating the model; analysts report conflicting descriptions in the founding texts, so models depend on the analyst. Naikar's 9-step procedure and expert review are the usual patches.
agent_test: Run the same S0 analysis with several samples; measure agreement between their level assignments.

claim: Work domain analysis was designed for stable, well-bounded technical systems; extensions are needed for automation (degree-of-automation layer), organisation (possibilities diagram) and teams.
agent_test: Add an S0 check: stable constraints or open-ended? Test routing by this.

claim: Even in Rasmussen's home domain tested evidence is scarce: of 49 nuclear workload-support studies only 11 evaluated workload empirically; the founding authors reported only preliminary support (snippet only).
agent_test: None; a caution against over-claiming.

claim: The DURESS-era experiments favoured the ecological (P+F) interface but the gain was mostly consistency and fault handling, not mean speed: six months of practice gave little difference in average performance while the physical-only group sometimes took up to 2 times longer (Christoffersen 1996 abstract). The 1995 report found faster detection, more accurate diagnosis and faster compensation. Pawlak and Vicente 1996 also found a P+F deficiency (no history information). A critique was published and no independent replication was found. N and effect sizes remain unobtained (full texts blocked).
agent_test: Re-open the original papers; the novel-fault finding is the one that matters for an S0 gate.

claim: Sorting a problem by how ordered it is (Cynefin-style) before choosing a strategy is proposed for complex problems; no empirical test.
agent_test: Test a four-way class label (clear, complicated, complex, chaotic) at S0 against no label.

claim: Perspective papers advise generative-AI interfaces to show several abstraction levels at once and map suggestions to their effects; no measurement of these recommendations exists in the sources read.
agent_test: Not an agent test; relevant to output format.

claim: LLM hierarchical task analysis is limited by grounding, not decomposition: ASHiTA beats other LLM pipelines (task accuracy 9.27 vs 4.88) but trails GPT given ground-truth labels (36.1).
agent_test: Check whether decomposition errors or missing facts drive failures on our own tasks.

claim: Pure extra input length lowers LLM reasoning (mean accuracy 0.92 to 0.68 at 3000 tokens of irrelevant padding, CoT does not fix it), and filler tokens give deployed LLMs no gain; so any gain from a scaffold must be shown against a length-matched generic control, which Wang 2024 and Kopka 2026 did not run.
agent_test: Compare the S0 prompt with a generic advice prompt of equal token count and with a no-S0 prompt.

claim: Abstraction-first and self-composed structure prompting beat CoT on reasoning benchmarks (Step-Back MMLU chemistry +11, TimeQA +27; Self-Discover T4D 69% vs 40% on PaLM 2-L), and most residual errors lie in later reasoning or computation (over 90% for Step-Back, 74.7% for Self-Discover MATH), not in the abstraction. Neither uses a multi-level means-ends hierarchy.
agent_test: Add a one-step abstraction at S0 and measure whether residual errors move from S0 to execution.

claim: LLMs label query ambiguity near chance in 2023-era tests (accuracy 50.37 to 54.25%; CoT and few-shot add little and can raise overconfidence), so a self-assigned problem class is unreliable unless measured; a wrong label needs a cheap exit.
agent_test: Measure the agent's own class-label accuracy against gold labels, then the harm from wrong labels.

claim: In 1,642 multi-agent traces failures split into specification and design 41.8%, coordination 36.9% and verification 21.3%; fixing role specification alone raised one system by 9.4%. Closest to a work-domain failure map, but not keyed to abstraction levels, and 'proceed on wrong assumptions' (6.8%) is a small share.
agent_test: Tag our own failures by MAST category and by hierarchy level and see which gate would have caught them.

claim: Benchmark and expert expectations overstate live gains: in a randomised trial of 246 real tasks developers expected a 24% speed-up and were 19% slower with AI; this is the AI-tool counterpart of the 75% vs 53% shrinkage in display studies.
agent_test: Keep a live-task holdout; expect smaller S0 gains there.

claim: No pooled effect size for ecological interface design exists in the sources found; the main review (McIlroy and Stanton 2015) covers how EID was applied (40% of applications omit the SRK taxonomy), not how well it worked. The only meta-analytic figure remains Wright 2019 on clinical displays.
agent_test: Treat human EID effect sizes as unknown; do not use them to size the agent effect.
